newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia wage fears based on worst case view.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia wage fears based on worst case view.

text.p: The one dark cloud on Australia's inflation horizon is wages growth, and there were signs that it may have been picking up towards the end of 1996.

A small rise in annual wages growth, some signs of a pick up in enterprise bargaining agreements and concerns over a union wage case had caused some fears over wages growth, but analysts said many outlooks had factored in worst case scenarios.
"The main uncertainty to the outlook for inflation (and for employment) remains labour costs," the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said in its quarterly report on the economy last week.
Final data on the pace of wages growth in the three months to November, due on Thursday, would also provide details on the pace of wages growth in the public and private sectors.
Data released earlier this month showed wages rose 1.2 percent in the November quarter.
In annual terms, they rose 0.1 percent to 3.9 percent, the first annual rise since August 1995.
The preliminary data was boosted by a large rise in female wages, which economists said suggested that public sector wages may have driven the quarterly rise.
Public sector wages growth, which was seen as less inflationary than private sector growth, had been stronger than private sector wages growth in recent quarters.

The RBA said this strength in public sector wages, which saw them rise 5.5 percent over the year to August compared to a 3.3 percent rise in private sector wages, was unusual as the bulk of enterprise bargains were for increases of about four percent.

The RBA said this might be the result of a compositional change in public sector employment, if recent cutbacks had mainly affected lower income earners. If this was the case, it may not be appropriate to draw strong conclusions from the data.

"Really it's the private sector (growth) that's going to be the key," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said. "If the public sector wages really represents classification differences, plus an an award to teachers, then maybe they're a one-off, they won't be quite as important in ongoing inflation," he said, but added this did not mean wages could be ignored.
Apart from the final average weekly earnings data, details on enterprise bargaining trends are due this week, and the union movement has a wage claim currently under consideration.

The union movements "living wage" claim asked for an 8.75 percent increase in award wages and three A$20 per week pay rises over three years. The RBA has warned that this claim would add around 1.6 percentage points to annual wages growth, and threaten employment for the unskilled, if it was granted.
However, many saw it as an ambit claim -- the unions had asked for more than they wanted so that they could concede some ground in negotiations but still receive what they want.
Accordingly, the end result was that the claim was expected to come out somewhere below what the union's were asking for and above the government's offer of three A$8 a week rises.
Bankers Trust senior economist Peter Munckton said the most likely outcome was a safety-net wage rise of around A$11-14, which would add around 0.4 percentage points to wages growth.
"Given some of the alternatives, the RBA would probably be sanguine about such an outcome," he said.
As well this week, data on enterprise agreements from the Department of Industrial Relations are due on Wednesday.
Last week, the RBA said the rate of wage rises in new agreements remained high, and economists said recent agreements suggested the pace of growth may be quickening.

"The news there is that they still seem to be running at around 4.5 to 5.0 percent, or a touch higher, and there some key agreements that do seem to be signaling that they do some to be picking up a little," National Australia Bank chief economist Jeff Oughton said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
